# Kaleidoscope

> Local memory for coding agents. Your agent forgets everything between sessions; Kaleidoscope gives it a memory that lives in a folder on your own machine and is shared by every editor and agent you use. Install it with `npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope`. It needs a key to run — email contact@kleosresearch.xyz.

- [Documentation](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/): what Kaleidoscope is, and which page answers your question
- [Getting started](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/getting-started/): install, activate with your key, and give a project a memory
- [Give your agent the skill](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/skill/): how an agent is told Kaleidoscope exists, and the four files it installs
- [Install](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/packages/): the package names and what is inside them
- [CLI reference](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/cli/): every `kscope` command and flag
- [MCP reference](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/mcp/): the two tools an agent sees, `search` and `remember`, and how to call them
- [Integrations](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/): Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, LangChain, LangGraph, Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, CrewAI, and any standard MCP client
- [Security](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/security/): what is isolated from what, what is not signed, and how to report a vulnerability
- [Privacy](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/privacy/): what stays on your machine, where a credential would be kept, and what this website itself does
- [Licenses and terms](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/legal/): Apache-2.0 and CC BY 4.0 are in force; the product terms are reviewed drafts, not yet adopted
- [Privacy notice](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/legal/privacy-notice/): a counsel-reviewed draft of the production privacy terms, not yet in force
- [Security policy](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/legal/security-policy/): a counsel-reviewed draft of the disclosure and supported-version policy, not yet in force
- [Support policy](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/legal/support-policy/): a counsel-reviewed draft of the support scope and response targets, not yet in force
- [Account](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/account/): you do not need an account, and you cannot create one yet
- [Operations](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/operations/): back up your memory, move it, uninstall, and delete a vault safely
- [Platforms](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/compatibility/): which platforms Kaleidoscope is for, and the one thing Windows does differently
- [Benchmarks](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/benchmarks/): two separate experiments — on the larger corpus, twelve times the memories at the same answer quality; on the smaller one, level with mem0 at 24% fewer tokens
- [Status](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/status/): whether anything is available, whether anything is down, and what has actually been run
- [Public agent skill](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/SKILL.md): how an agent should retrieve and write memory
- [Agent instructions](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/agent-instructions.md): the short pointers Kaleidoscope installs into AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or a Cursor rule
- [Status record](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/status.json): the same status these pages state, in machine-readable form
- [Platform support record](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/platform-support.json): which platforms have been run on and which have only had a compiler check
- [Full CLI help text](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/reference/kaleidoscope-cli.txt): the complete `kaleidoscope` help output
- [Tool reference](https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/reference/kaleidoscope-mcp.json): the fields of the two tools an agent sees

Kaleidoscope is installable today: `npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope` gives you the `kscope` command on macOS and Linux, on both Apple Silicon and x86_64. It needs a key to run. We send keys by email — write to contact@kleosresearch.xyz. Windows is not supported: creating a vault there is refused on purpose until the filesystem work lands.

Once it is installed, `kscope init` in a project creates the memory and connects whichever agent you use. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, standard MCP clients and the agent frameworks all read the same vault. Two of those connections have a limit worth stating: Codex's configuration entry is written and removed exactly, but Codex offers no way to confirm it then starts the server, and Cursor's has never been checked by launching Cursor itself. The agent frameworks were tested against stand-in models rather than a live provider.

What is not here: hosted memory does not exist -- there is no service, endpoint, API or waitlist, and nothing syncs your memory anywhere. It stays in a folder in your project. Apache-2.0 covers the public code and CC BY 4.0 covers this documentation, and both are in force; the engine licence, privacy notice, security policy and support policy have been reviewed by counsel but not adopted, so none of them is yet in force and there is no support commitment. Nothing is signed for release. The part that stores and searches your memory ships as proprietary object code, and its source is not public. Benchmark results are described in plain words on the benchmarks page; the full benchmark method is not published yet.

---

# Kaleidoscope

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Local memory for agents · one vault · every tool

  Your agent forgets. This is where it remembers.

  Every new session, your coding agent starts from nothing. It re-asks questions you already answered, re-reads code it already understood, and repeats mistakes you already paid for. Kaleidoscope gives it a memory that stays on your machine and follows you between tools.

  Your agent gets two things it can do: look something up, and write something down. Everything it stores lives in a folder in your project. No server, no account, and nothing leaves your disk.

    Get started
    Give your agent the skill
    What works today

## Install it

```bash
npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope
```

Then activate it with your key and give a project a memory:

```bash
export KALEIDOSCOPE_API_KEY=<your key>
kscope activate
cd ~/your-project && kscope init
```

You need a key to run it. Email contact@kleosresearch.xyz
and we will send you one. Full walkthrough in
getting started.

## What you get

**It stays on your machine.** Your memory is a folder inside your project. The
part that stores and searches it runs on your laptop and needs no network, so
what you write down is not something we can read.

**One memory, every tool.** Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode all read the
same vault. Something your agent learned in one of them is there in the next.

**Your agent drives it.** `kscope init` wires up whichever tool you use, and
from then on you just talk normally — ask it what you decided last week, or tell
it to remember something. The two commands it uses are the only two it sees.

## Where to go next

- Getting started — install, activate, and give a
  project a memory.
- Give your agent the skill — a file that teaches an agent how
  to use its memory well.
- What works today — which platforms and tools are covered.
- Documentation — everything else.

---

# Kaleidoscope documentation

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Kaleidoscope is local memory for agents. Your memory lives in a vault on your
machine, and every editor or agent you connect shares one profile through a
command-line tool and a long-lived process that offers exactly two tools.

Install it with `npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope`. You need a key to
run it — email contact@kleosresearch.xyz and
we will send you one. There is no account to create and no sign-in.
What works today is the plain answer to what is covered.

## Start here

- Getting started — install it, activate your key, and
  give a project a memory.
- Give your agent the skill — the file that tells an agent
  Kaleidoscope exists, what it writes into your instruction file, and the four
  files offered for download.
- Install — the one command that installs it, what lands on
  your disk, and what your machine needs.
- Concepts — profile, vault, engine, manager, account: which
  is which, and which owns what.

## The command line

- CLI overview — the whole `kscope` surface grouped by what each
  command is for, the flags there are, and the safety invariants that govern
  every subcommand.
- Profiles and vaults — `init`, `init-profile`, the
  `profile` commands, and `where`.
- Connect an editor — `kscope init`, and what it writes
  into your editor's configuration.
- Agent instructions — the instruction file and the
  skill `kscope init` installs, and where each editor reads them from.
- Diagnostics — `where`, `gate`, `model` and
  `call doctor`.
- Account commands — the account surface, none of which
  ships, and `activate`, which is what there is instead.

Several verbs written down elsewhere are not in the command you can install.
`connect`, `disconnect`, `config`, `doctor`, `teardown`, `profile use`,
`instructions install` and every account command belong to a separate
`kaleidoscope` executable that is published on no channel, so they are commands
you cannot obtain rather than commands you can run. What ships in their place is
`kscope init`, which does the wiring and installs the instruction file and the
skill itself, and `kscope call doctor`, which is the diagnostic.

- MCP — the two tools a model sees, their fields, and a correct
  call of each.
- Editors, agents and frameworks — find yours and the one
  command that connects it.

  different things "remove Kaleidoscope" can mean.

  it never touches.

  happen, and what causes each.

# Account and devices

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/account/
Updated: 2026-08-30

You do not need an account to use Kaleidoscope — your memory lives on your
machine and works without one. You also could not sign in today if you wanted
to: every command that reaches the account service answers
`provider not configured`, because no sign-in service is configured or
published.

## What signing in would be for

Signing in is designed as an ordinary browser sign-in, with a code-based path
for machines that have no browser. It manages your product account and the
devices attached to it. It is not a connection to hosted memory: no hosted
service, endpoint, API, waitlist, or sync path exists, and signing in would not
opt you into one.

## What it never does to your memory

Signing in never uploads, syncs, analyses, trains on, or deletes your memory.
Memory content, your queries, the results you got back, memory IDs, graph data,
local paths, and vault locations are all excluded from the account protocol, and
the account client rejects those fields — and any absolute local path — before
anything would leave your machine.

## Where a sign-in credential would be kept

Signing in is not built yet, so nothing is stored anywhere today. When it is,
the refresh credential goes to the operating system's own credential store — the
login Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows, the Secret Service on
Linux — and never into a file we write, into an editor's configuration, or into
a profile. On Linux, if no secret service is running, signing in stops and tells
you rather than falling back to something weaker.

One caveat we would rather state than let you discover: on macOS, whether the
system remembers your approval depends on the program being signed with a stable
identity. Kaleidoscope is not signed for release,
so an unsigned build can be asked for your login password every time it reaches
the Keychain. That is a property of unsigned software, not of how the credential
is stored, and it goes away when signed builds ship.

Signing in is only ever about your account and your devices. It does not upload,
sync, analyse, train on or delete your memory, and it does not connect you to a
hosted service — there isn't one.

An **alpha key is not a sign-in and does not use the Keychain at all.** It is
read from an environment variable or from a file you write yourself, and it
never prompts for your login password. See
if you have an alpha key.

## What logging out changes

Logging out removes or revokes your credentials, according to the scope you
chose. It does not change which profile you are on and it does not alter a
single byte of your vault. Deleting a vault is a separate, explicit operation
with its own confirmation — see Operations.

## The commands

Every account command, with what each one does and does not do, is on
the account command page.

---

# Benchmarks

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/benchmarks/
Release: 0.0.5
Updated: 2026-08-30

Kaleidoscope is measured on BEAM, a public benchmark for long-term memory in
conversation. The results below are ours: we ran them, on our machines, against
a named alternative. There is no build you can download yet, so you cannot
reproduce them yourself today. Read them with that in mind.

These are **separate experiments**, run on different corpora and different sets
of questions. Each section says which. They answer different questions and are
not steps in one series, so please do not read them as one.

## Twelve times the memories, the same answer quality

*The larger of the two corpora: about seventy-five thousand memories over
thirty-five conversations.*

We grew the store from about six thousand memories to about seventy-five
thousand, spread across thirty-five separate vaults, and ran the questions for
that larger corpus. It scored **0.73** on BEAM's scale, where 1.0 is a perfect
answer to every question — the same score the same configuration reached on the
smaller corpus. Nothing
degraded as the store filled up.

Retrieving a hundred memories for each question instead of fifty changed
nothing either. Past a point, handing the reader more does not help; handing it
the right thing does.

That is the property that matters for memory you mean to keep for years. A store
that answers well when it is empty and badly when it is full is not memory.

## Far better than answering with no memory

*The smaller corpus: twenty conversations. Everything in this section and the
next was measured there, with the same reader and the same judge throughout.*

A model answering with nothing to go on gets most of these questions wrong. With
Kaleidoscope it answers most of them well. This is the largest single difference
in anything we have measured.

Putting the whole conversation into the context window instead does not answer
better than retrieving from memory, and it costs about a hundred and thirty
thousand tokens a question to do it. More context is not the same as the right
context.

## Level with mem0, at a quarter fewer tokens

*Same smaller corpus, same twenty conversations.*

We ran mem0's own system on those conversations, using mem0's own prompt and
mem0's own judge, and compared it with ours. **The answer quality matches.** Ours
gets there on **8,173 prompt tokens a question against mem0's 10,762 — 24%
fewer.**

We are not claiming to beat mem0. On this benchmark the two are level, and the
difference is what it costs to get there. mem0 has never published a BEAM score
of its own; the number above is our measurement of their system, not theirs.

## Writing is fast when you write in batches

At ten thousand memories in a vault, storing a memory takes about **76
milliseconds**.\* That is measured end to end — starting the process, opening
the vault, admitting the memory and refreshing the index — not just the part
inside the engine.

\* Writing twenty at a time. A single write on its own costs far more, because
most of the cost is paid once per call rather than once per memory. Batch your
writes.

## What we have not measured

Everything here comes from one benchmark on one kind of workload: long,
multi-session conversations. We have not measured code repositories, documents,
or anything else you might point memory at.

We also chose the settings we ran by trying them against the very questions we
then scored, without holding a set of questions back, so treat all of this as
our best case rather than a promise. The full method — every arm, every
measurement, and the ones that did not work — will be published alongside the
first release.

---

# CLI reference

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/cli/
Updated: 2026-08-30

The command you will run is `kscope`. It sets up your local memory,
connects your editor or agent to it, and tells you what is wrong when something
does not work. Read this as the reference for the
command surface rather than a set of steps to follow now.

`kscope` is the whole of Kaleidoscope you can install: the engine that stores
and searches your memory, with the setup half of the manager compiled into the
same executable. There is no second command to install beside it, and nothing
here asks you to run one.

There is a second executable, `kaleidoscope`, and it is where several verbs you
may have seen written down actually live: `connect`, `disconnect`, `config`,
`doctor`, `teardown`, `profile use`, `instructions install` and the whole
account surface. It is built only from source and is published on no channel, so
those are commands you cannot obtain rather than commands you can run. Where a
page here describes one, it says so.

Read the full `kscope` help text.

## The commands, by what they are for

| | |
|---|---|
| Profiles and vaults | `init`, `init-profile`, `profile create`, `import`, `list`, `show`, `remove`, `launch`, `where` |
| Connect an editor | `init` |
| Agent instructions | `init` |
| Diagnostics | `where`, `gate`, `model`, `vault-verify`, `call doctor` |
| Account and devices | nothing that ships; `activate` is what there is |

`kscope init` is the command that sets you up, which is why it appears three
times: it creates the vault, and then it tells every agent on this
machine that the vault exists — the memory server, the instruction file, and the
skill, once per agent.

Two groups have no page of their own. The vault lifecycle commands —
`vault-migrate`, `vault-verify`, `vault-preview`, `vault-delete`, and the frozen
macOS preview of encrypted repository vaults — belong with
Operations. The four commands that address a vault
directly, `mcp`, `serve`, `context` and `call`, belong with the
MCP reference; the help text is exhaustive about how each of them
decides which vault it means.

## The flags there are

`--profile NAME` names the vault to work in. `mcp`, `serve`, `context` and
`call` take it, it is what an editor or agent is started with, and nothing
else accepts it. `kscope init` does not: it works on the directory you are in,
or on a root you name as a positional argument.

`--no-wire` makes `kscope init` create the vault and stop, for someone who keeps
host configuration under their own control. It works on the build that ships,
although `--help` does not list it.

`--root-only` narrows `kscope where` to the vault root and the project it was
resolved from. `--cross-backend` widens `kscope vault-verify`.

`--help` and `--version` print the surface and the version; `-h` and `-V` are
accepted for both.

There is no `--engine`, no `--dry-run` and no `--yes` on this executable, and no
`--profile`, `--root`, `--host`, `--scope` or `--project` on `kscope init`.
Those are flags of the unpublished manager. An unrecognised argument is not an
error you can act on: `kscope` prints its help text and leaves everything alone.

## Where the wiring goes, and why

The memory server entry goes in your home directory — `~/.claude.json`,
`~/.codex/config.toml`, `~/.cursor/mcp.json`,
`~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`. That is not a default you can change on the
shipped build; it is the only behaviour it has. The reason is that an agent
agent usually runs your work in a git worktree or a temporary clone, and an
entry stored inside one project directory is not read from there at all.

The instruction file and the skill go the other way, always into the project:
git is what carries them into that worktree or clone, and a `CLAUDE.md` in your
home directory would inject Kaleidoscope into every unrelated project you ever
open.

## What holds for everything that writes

These hold for every file `kscope init` touches, not just one of them.

- Kaleidoscope writes only the block it owns, marked by an ownership comment on
  either side wherever the file format has room for comments, and it leaves a
  receipt beside every file it wrote — `config.toml.kaleidoscope-owner.json`
  beside a host configuration, `CLAUDE.md.kaleidoscope-instruction-owner.json`
  beside an instruction file.
- If what it finds no longer matches that receipt — because you edited inside
  the markers, or wrote an entry of your own by hand — it stops at that file,
  changes nothing there, and reports that one step as failed by name. The other
  steps still happen: a Cursor rule it cannot write must not cost you your
  Claude Code registration.
- A file it changes rather than creates is copied first, to
  `.kaleidoscope-backup` beside it, and the rest of the file is left
  exactly as it was.
- The configuration written for your editor or agent contains no tokens, no
  provider keys, and no vault location. It names this executable, a profile, and
  the two tools `search` and `remember`.
- Running `kscope init` again is safe. A root that is already a vault is left
  exactly as it is — it says so, and touches nothing inside it — while the
  wiring is re-checked and repaired.
- The account boundary other pages describe needs no policing here. This
  executable carries no account commands, so there is no account traffic to keep
  away from your memory in the first place.

---

# Account commands

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/cli/account/
Updated: 2026-08-30

None of the commands on this page ships. Every one of them belongs to
`kaleidoscope`, the manager executable, which is built from source and published
on no channel — so they are not commands that fail for you, they are commands you
cannot obtain. Even built from source they would go no further: each one that
reaches the account service answers `provider not configured`, because no sign-in
service is configured or published either.

They are written down here so you can see the shape of what signing in will and
will not do when it arrives.

## What there is instead

The alpha is opened by a key, not by an account. Email
contact@kleosresearch.xyz for one, and then:

```bash
kscope activate
```

`activate` takes the key from `KALEIDOSCOPE_API_KEY`, from the key file, or from
standard input; stores it at the path `kscope gate` reports, so an engine your
editor starts with an empty environment still finds it; and waits for the verdict
rather than leaving the next command to discover an empty cache. It is the whole
of the account-shaped surface on the executable you installed.

You do not need an account to use Kaleidoscope. Your memory lives on your machine
and has never needed one.

## The surface, when it arrives

Everything from here down is `kaleidoscope`, not `kscope`. None of it runs on the
command you have.

### Sign in and out

```bash
kaleidoscope login
kaleidoscope login --device
kaleidoscope status --json
kaleidoscope logout
kaleidoscope logout --all-devices
kaleidoscope logout --local-only
```

`login` is an ordinary browser sign-in; `--device` is the code-based path for a
machine with no browser.

`logout` removes or revokes your credentials according to the scope you chose.
`--all-devices` ends every session on the account; `--local-only` removes the
credential from this machine and warns you that it has not revoked anything
remotely. Neither changes which profile a command resolves to, and neither alters
a byte of your vault.

`kaleidoscope status` reports your account session on this machine. It is not
related to the status page, which is about what is available.

### Linked sign-in providers

```bash
kaleidoscope account link PROVIDER
kaleidoscope account identities
kaleidoscope account unlink EXTERNAL_IDENTITY_UUID
kaleidoscope account revoke-session
```

`account identities` is where you get the opaque UUID that `account unlink`
needs; it lists those IDs and nothing else.

`account revoke-session` has the deliberately narrow meaning of revoking the
session you are currently using. It does not deactivate an account.

### Devices

```bash
kaleidoscope devices list
kaleidoscope devices revoke DEVICE_UUID
```

The devices attached to your account, and how to detach one. Revoking a device is
an account operation; the vault on that device is untouched.

### Local account reference

```bash
kaleidoscope profile account show [NAME]
kaleidoscope profile account bind ACCOUNT_UUID [NAME]
kaleidoscope profile account unbind [NAME]
```

These three would work offline, because they never leave your machine: they write
a non-secret account ID into a local profile and nothing more — no engine
started, no service contacted, no vault touched, no credential stored. They are
still manager commands, so they are still not commands you can run.

## The boundary

On the executable that ships there is no boundary to police, because there is no
account traffic: `kscope` carries no account commands at all, and `activate`
speaks only about your key.

In the manager, account traffic goes to a closed list of account-only routes and
never touches the memory engine. A guard rejects memory fields, profile fields
and absolute local paths before anything is sent.

What signing in would mean, and where a credential would be kept:
Account and devices.

---

# Connect an editor or agent

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/cli/connect/
Updated: 2026-08-30

One command does both jobs. `kscope init`, run inside a project, creates that
project's memory and writes the entry your editor or agent needs to find it.

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
```

It tells you what it did, line by line: the vault it created, the `.gitignore`
rule it added, and then a step for each thing it wired — the memory server
registered with an agent, the instruction file written for it, and the skill
installed where that agent reads skills. It knows Claude Code, Codex, Cursor
and OpenCode, and it wires the ones whose configuration directory already exists
on this machine. If it recognises none of them it writes an `AGENTS.md` instead,
which most other agents will read, and says so.

Restart your editor afterwards. Until you do, it is still running with the
configuration it started with.

## The profile the entry names

The entry `kscope init` writes starts this executable with `--profile default`,
and creating the vault does not create that profile. Write it once, naming the
vault `init` just made:

```bash
kscope profile import default ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope
```

Until that profile exists, anything started with `--profile default` refuses
with `profile does not exist`, and the refusal is all your editor will show you.
Profiles and vaults has the rest of it.

## It will not overwrite your work

Kaleidoscope only touches the block it owns, and it leaves a receipt beside each
one. If it finds a Kaleidoscope entry that does not match its receipt — because
you edited it, or added one by hand — it stops, changes nothing, and tells you
which file to look at. That is the intended behaviour, not a failure: the
alternative is silently replacing something you wrote on purpose.

## Removing it

There is no `disconnect` on the command you have. The verb exists, but only in
`kaleidoscope`, the manager executable, which is built from source and published
on no channel — so removing the wiring is something you do by hand. Everything
`kscope init` writes is marked and receipted so that you can.

The memory server entry is in your home directory, one file per agent: the
`kaleidoscope` entry under `mcpServers` in `~/.claude.json`, in
`~/.cursor/mcp.json` and in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`, and the block
between the `kaleidoscope-manager` marker comments in `~/.codex/config.toml`.
Delete the entry or the marked block, and the `.kaleidoscope-owner.json` receipt
beside the file, which is the record of what was put there.

The instruction file and the skill are in the project: the marked block in
`CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`, `.claude/skills/use-kaleidoscope/` for Claude Code,
`.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/` for Codex and OpenCode, and
`.cursor/rules/kaleidoscope.mdc` for Cursor. Each of those has a receipt beside
it too. `npm uninstall -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope` removes the command
itself, and nothing else.

None of that touches your memory, and none of it needs to: unwiring an editor is
not a way to delete a vault, and deleting a vault is not a way to unwire an
editor. An entry pointing at a vault that no longer exists is harmless, and
re-running `kscope init` writes the wiring back.

Operations covers moving a vault, backing it up, and
deleting one on purpose.

---

# Diagnostics

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/cli/diagnostics/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Four questions come up when something looks wrong. A command answers each, and
none of those commands reads or changes a single memory.

## Where is my memory?

```bash
kscope where
```

Prints the vault this directory resolves to, and the workspace it belongs to.
Run it when you are not sure which project's memory your agent is talking to.

## Is my key working?

```bash
kscope gate
```

Says whether this build checks a licence, which commands need one, and where it
looks for your key. If a command has been refused, this is the page that tells
you why in one line.

```bash
kscope activate
```

Re-checks the key you already have and stores it. `"entitled":true` means you
are set up.

## Is the engine complete?

```bash
kscope model
```

Should print `"status":"bundled"`. Anything else means the part that understands
what your memories mean is missing, and search will quietly get worse rather
than fail — which is why it is worth checking directly.

## Is my vault healthy?

```bash
kscope vault-verify /path/to/.kaleidoscope
```

Counts what is stored and reports whether the copies agree. It reads only.

For a deeper report, `call doctor` runs the full diagnostic and returns JSON.
Like every `call`, it reads one JSON request from standard input, and `inspect`
is the mode that only looks:

```bash
echo '{"mode":"inspect"}' | kscope call doctor
```

It is an operator command, so your agent is never offered it.

---

# Agent instructions

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/cli/instructions/
Updated: 2026-08-30

An agent only uses memory if something told it to. Kaleidoscope writes two
things into your project for that: a short marked block in whichever instruction
file your agent already reads, and the skill itself. It is the same pair shown
in give your agent the skill, which offers both files for
download.

There is no separate command for it, and no flag to remember. `kscope init`
installs them as part of the run that creates the vault, once for each agent
it finds:

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
```

The steps go past as it works — `claude for claude-code`, `skill for
claude-code`, `agents for codex`, one line each, and a named failure if one of
them could not be written.

## Where each agent reads them

The skill directory is not the same for every agent, and a skill written to
the wrong one is a file the agent silently never loads. `kscope init` writes
the path the agent in front of it actually reads.

| agent | instruction file | skill |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | a marked block in `CLAUDE.md` | `.claude/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md` |
| Codex | a marked block in `AGENTS.md` | `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md` |
| OpenCode | a marked block in `AGENTS.md` | `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md` |
| Cursor | `.cursor/rules/kaleidoscope.mdc`, the whole file | none: Cursor has no skill directory |
| none detected | a marked block in `AGENTS.md` | none |

All of it goes into the project, and none of it into your home directory. Git is
what carries these files into the worktree or the temporary clone an agent
agent usually runs your work in, and a `CLAUDE.md` in your home directory would
inject Kaleidoscope into every unrelated project you ever open.

## Installing one on its own, and taking one back out

`kaleidoscope instructions install TARGET` and `instructions remove TARGET` are
the commands for writing one of these files at a time, or removing one exactly.
They belong to `kaleidoscope`, the manager executable, which is built from source
and published on no channel: you cannot install it, so you cannot run them. On
the command that ships, installing is something `kscope init` does for you and
removing is done by hand — connect an editor or
agent lists the files to look in.

## Why the block has markers

Everything appended to an existing file sits between two ownership comments, and
every file Kaleidoscope owns outright gets a receipt beside it. That pair is what
makes a second `kscope init` idempotent instead of duplicating, what makes an
exact removal possible, and what is read before the file is touched at all. If
you have edited the text between the markers, that one step stops and hands the
file back rather than overwriting your work — and the remaining steps still run,
because a Cursor rule that cannot be written must not cost you your Claude Code
registration.

---

# Profiles and vaults

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/cli/profiles/
Updated: 2026-08-30

A vault is one memory store on your machine: a directory at a path you chose. A
profile is a name for one of them — an absolute root, the three identifiers
inside it, and the durability, written where this executable can find them again.
An editor or agent is started with a profile name; nothing else is.

## Create a vault

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
```

`init` with nothing after it resolves the root — `KSCOPE_ROOT`, else
`.kaleidoscope/` under the repository's main checkout, else `.kaleidoscope/`
under the working directory — creates the vault there, and prints the path it
chose along with where the path came from, so a default you did not type is
never silent. A root that is already a vault is left exactly as it is, and told
about rather than initialised over. Add `--no-wire` to create the vault and stop
there, without touching any editor's configuration.

```bash
kscope init /absolute/path/to/vault 2026-08-30T09:00:00Z
```

Naming the root and an RFC 3339 timestamp is the form for a program that has to
control the moment a vault records as its creation. It makes the vault and stops;
it wires nothing.

Durability is the last word on either form, and `process-local` is both the
default and the only value any release has accepted. Asking for the other one:

```bash
kscope init durable-local
```

is refused, and the refusal is worth reading rather than working around:
`durable-local is not available in this build, so nothing was created`. It is a
property of the build and not of your machine or your disk, and the engine says
so — it refuses before writing anything rather than quietly giving you
`process-local` under a stronger name. What `process-local` promises is that a
vault stays complete-or-absent across a process crash or a hard kill; it makes
no promise about a write acknowledged in the moment before the machine loses
power.

## Name a vault, so an editor can be started with it

```bash
kscope profile import default ~/your-project/.kaleidoscope
kscope init-profile work /absolute/path/to/vault 2026-08-30T09:00:00Z
kscope profile create work /absolute/path/to/vault WORKSPACE_ID PRINCIPAL_ID JOURNAL
```

`profile import` reads the identity out of a vault that already exists and writes
it under the name you give. It is the one to run after `kscope init`, and it is
how the profile called `default` comes to exist: the wiring `init` writes names
that profile, and creating a vault does not create it. Until it does exist,
anything started with `--profile default` refuses with `profile does not exist`.

`init-profile` is the same two things in the other order — it initialises the root
you name and then writes the profile. If the second step fails it does not delete
the vault it has just committed; the refusal reports the exact root and the
`kscope profile import` command that finishes the job.

`profile create` takes the identifiers explicitly and verifies them against the
vault, for a caller that already holds them. `kscope where` is where they come
from for a vault you have.

Neither one creates or relocates canonical vault data, and none of the three
stores a secret. A profile is a pointer.

## List, inspect, remove

```bash
kscope profile list
kscope profile show default
kscope profile launch default
kscope profile remove work
```

`profile list` shows the profiles this machine knows, each validated against its
vault as it is read. `profile show` prints one of them. `profile launch` prints
the launch descriptor an editor entry is made of: this executable's absolute
path, `mcp --profile NAME`, and the two tool names `search` and `remember`. It
carries no vault coordinates and no key.

`profile remove` forgets a profile. It does not delete the vault the profile
pointed at — your memory is a directory on your disk and it stays there. Getting
rid of the memory itself is a separate, deliberate act; see
Operations.

## There is no active profile

Nothing on this executable makes one profile current. `profile use` is a
manager command, and the manager is published on no channel, so there is neither
a `kscope profile use` to run nor anything that would remember the answer.

A command that names no profile is not lost, though. `mcp`, `serve`, `context`
and `call` resolve a vault from where you are, by the same rules `init` uses, and
`where` prints the address they will arrive at before you rely on it.

```bash
kscope where
```

## Binding a profile to an account

`profile account show`, `bind` and `unbind` write a local, non-secret account
reference into a profile and nothing more. They are manager commands too, so they
are not on the executable you installed. The command that ships carries nothing
account-shaped except `kscope activate`, which stores your key; the rest is on
the account page.

## What a profile is not

It is not a copy of your memory, and it is not a credential store. Deleting a
profile, naming a different one, or reinstalling Kaleidoscope leaves every byte
of every vault exactly where it was.

---

# Platforms

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/compatibility/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Kaleidoscope targets macOS on Apple Silicon and Intel, Linux on x86_64 and
arm64, and Windows on x86_64 and arm64.

**Four of those six are published today**, and `npm install -g
@kleos-research/kaleidoscope` brings down the one built for your machine. You
need a key to run it, and nothing is signed for release. Windows is the platform
on the list you cannot install on yet. What is available today.

| platform | architectures | today |
|---|---|---|
| macOS | Apple Silicon, Intel | published on npm |
| Linux | x86_64, arm64 | published on npm |
| Windows | x86_64, arm64 | no package published |

## Windows creates no vault

On Windows, creating a new vault is refused on purpose. Windows needs its own
filesystem work first — file locking, link handling, and flushing writes all the
way to the disk — and until that lands Kaleidoscope stops rather than writing
memory it cannot stand behind.

This is a deliberate refusal in the code, not a gap, and it is the one platform
fact worth knowing before you plan around it. There is no Windows package
published for the install to bring down in the first place, and the rest of the
Windows work is outstanding too, so do not read the refusal as the only thing
between you and a working install there.

## What has actually been run

Kaleidoscope is built and published for four platforms — macOS on Apple Silicon
and x86_64, and Linux on arm64 and x86_64 — and you can install and run it on
any of them. We have run it ourselves on one: a Mac with Apple Silicon. Built
and published is not the same as tried by hand, and the difference is worth
knowing.
The full account is on the status page.

---

# Concepts and boundaries

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/concepts/
Updated: 2026-08-30

The boundary that matters is your local memory versus your account metadata —
not merely whether you are signed in.

## Local engine

The proprietary native engine owns the memory algorithm, the canonical vault on
your machine, the graph, ranking, and the stdio MCP behavior. Its source is not
part of the public CLI, client, integration, or skill surfaces.

## Manager and profile

The manager is the half of Kaleidoscope that sets things up rather than storing
anything, and most of it is compiled into the `kscope` command you install.
`kscope init` creates a vault, edits host configuration safely, and installs
agent guidance; `kscope profile create`, `import`, `list`, `show` and `remove`
manage profiles; `kscope profile launch` prints the engine launch descriptor a
host is started with; and `kscope call doctor` is the offline diagnostic.

The account and device half is not in that command. Signing in, binding a
profile to an account, and listing or revoking devices belong to a separate
`kaleidoscope` executable, which is published on no channel — so those are
commands you cannot obtain, rather than commands you can run. A profile may hold
one explicit account UUID reference locally; that changes neither its vault
identity nor its credentials.

## What gets installed

You install one package, `@kleos-research/kaleidoscope` from npm, and it brings
in a second package built for your platform. The npm package holds the full
public client, the typed resolver that finds the installed payload, and the
`kscope` command. The platform package holds a single program: the proprietary
engine as object code, with the setup half of the manager compiled into it.
Neither one contains engine source, and neither downloads anything at install
time.

A Python package is intended and not published. `kscope-memory` on PyPI is a
0.0.0 placeholder that says so itself, so there is no Python route in today.

## One profile, every tool

Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, framework clients, and generic MCP clients
are consumers of the same profile. They do not become separate memory stores
merely because their configuration formats differ.

## Account identity

Signing in is designed to link a product account and a device. None of it is
something you can do today: there is no service to sign in to, and the commands
that would do it are in the manager executable that is published on no channel.
The account protocol rejects memory fields and absolute local paths before
transport. Signing out or unlinking is not a vault operation, and must not be
read as consent to upload memory.

## Hosted memory

A hosted service is a later product requiring separate authorization, tenant
isolation, retention, residency, deletion, sync, billing, and incident-response
contracts. It does not exist, and signing in does not opt you into it.

---

# Getting started

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/getting-started/
Release: 0.0.5
Updated: 2026-08-30

Four steps. They take about two minutes, and the third one is where the useful
part happens.

You need macOS or Linux and Node.js 18 or newer.

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope
```

This gives you the `kscope` command. It also pulls in a second package built
for your platform, which carries the part that stores and searches your memory.

## 2. Activate it with your key

Kaleidoscope needs a key to run. If you do not have one, email
contact@kleosresearch.xyz.

```bash
export KALEIDOSCOPE_API_KEY=<your key>
kscope activate
```

You should see `"entitled":true` and a fragment of your key. `activate` also
saves the key, so that `export` is a one-off — new terminals will find it.

If you would rather not put the key in your shell at all, write it into a file
by hand instead. On macOS that is
`~/Library/Application Support/kaleidoscope/entitlement/api-key`; on Linux it is
the same path under `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, or `~/.config`. The file holds the key
and nothing else, and it must be readable only by you (`chmod 600`).

## 3. Give a project a memory

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
```

This creates the vault — a `.kaleidoscope` folder in your project, added to your
`.gitignore` — and wires up whichever agent you use. It knows Claude Code,
Codex, Cursor and OpenCode, and it writes an `AGENTS.md` for anything else.

For each agent it finds, it registers the memory server in that agent's own
configuration and writes the instruction file that agent reads — a marked block
in `CLAUDE.md` for Claude Code, in `AGENTS.md` for Codex and OpenCode, and the
whole of `.cursor/rules/kaleidoscope.mdc` for Cursor. Those three also get the
`use-kaleidoscope` skill installed where they look for skills; Cursor has
nowhere to put one, so it gets the rule file and nothing more. It prints what it
wired and then each step it took, so what changed is on your screen rather than
left for you to find later.

If you would rather write those entries yourself, `kscope init --no-wire`
creates the vault and leaves every configuration file alone.

It only touches the part of your editor's configuration that belongs to
Kaleidoscope. If it finds a Kaleidoscope entry someone added by hand, it stops
and tells you rather than overwriting your work.

## 4. Restart your agent, then just talk to it

Your agent now has two things it can do: look something up, and write something
down. You do not call those yourself. Ask it what you decided about a design
last week, or tell it to remember that you prefer a particular approach, and it
will use them.

If it does not seem to know its memory is there, the most reliable fix is to
give it the skill — a short file that teaches it when to read
and when to write. Otherwise, see
Troubleshooting.

## Removing it

Your memory is a folder. Deleting `.kaleidoscope` from a project deletes that
project's memory and nothing else; `npm uninstall -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope`
removes the command and leaves every vault alone.
Operations covers moving and inspecting a vault.

---

# Editors, agents and frameworks

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Every editor and agent below talks to the same engine on your machine, over one
long-lived process, and sees exactly two tools: `search` and `remember`. Connect
five of them and they share one memory instead of starting five stores.

One command wires the editors. `kscope init`, run inside a project, creates that
project's vault and then wires every agent whose own configuration
directory already exists on this machine. What it writes is different for each
one — a different configuration file, a different instruction file, a different
place a skill lives — and that difference is what the pages below set out.

| | wired by |
|---|---|
| Claude Code | `kscope init`, in the project |
| Codex | `kscope init`, in the project |
| Cursor | `kscope init`, in the project |
| OpenCode | `kscope init`, in the project |
| Any other MCP client | the descriptor from `kscope profile launch NAME` |

Frameworks connect through their own MCP adapter, using the same descriptor:
Claude Agent SDK ·
OpenAI Agents SDK ·
LangChain ·
LangGraph ·
CrewAI

The build these pages describe is the one that is published:
`npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope` gives you `kscope` today, and
running it needs a key. Install covers both steps.
What has actually been run, and on what.

`kscope init` also installs the skill that tells your agent when to read its
memory and when to write to it — for Cursor, a project rule instead. What that
document says, and how to install it by hand, is on
give your agent the skill.

---

# Claude Agent SDK

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/claude-agent-sdk/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Create one Claude Agent SDK client for the run you intend, and hand it a stdio
MCP configuration that names the Kaleidoscope tools explicitly. One client, one
process, for the whole run.

## Connect it

```bash
kscope profile launch default
```

`default` there is a profile name, and the profile has to exist before it can
be printed — see profiles and vaults.

Put that descriptor in the SDK's own stdio MCP configuration. One client, opened
around the run and closed at the end — not a fresh engine process per tool call.

## What it writes

Nothing on your disk. The descriptor sets an empty environment for the child
process, so account tokens, vault locations and provider keys never reach it.
Your model-provider credentials stay in your own application.

## The one thing that is different here

The tool allowlist is two names, and you write them out:

```text
mcp__kaleidoscope__search
mcp__kaleidoscope__remember
```

Anything else is not a Kaleidoscope tool. Operator commands are never offered to
a model, so there is no third name to add.

## Disconnect

Close the client. Remove the descriptor from your SDK configuration; nothing
else was changed.

---

# Claude Code

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/claude-code/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Claude Code is wired by the same command as everything else. `kscope init`, run
in a project, sees Claude Code on this machine and does three things for it:
registers the memory server, writes the instruction block, and installs the
skill. Everything it writes is marked as its own, so you can find it again.

## Wire it

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
```

Claude Code counts as present when `~/.claude` or `~/.claude.json` exists. Both
are written by Claude Code itself, and neither is a path this command would
create on its way to looking, so its absence means Claude Code is left alone
rather than given a configuration file it never asked for.

## What it writes

The MCP entry goes in `~/.claude.json`, under `mcpServers` as `kaleidoscope`:
`"type": "stdio"`, this executable's absolute path, and the arguments
`mcp --profile default`. That file is Claude Code's own live configuration and
is usually large; only the entry Kaleidoscope owns is written, the rest comes
back as it was, and a receipt is left beside it in
`~/.claude.json.kaleidoscope-owner.json`.

The instruction block goes in `CLAUDE.md` in the project, between
`kaleidoscope-manager` marker comments, with the rest of the file untouched.

The skill goes in `.claude/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md` in the project.
That is where Claude Code looks for a skill; it does not read `.agents/skills/`,
which is why this path differs from the one Codex and OpenCode get.

The server those entries start publishes only `search` and `remember`. Nothing
written carries your vault location, a provider key, or an account credential.

Restart Claude Code afterwards. Until you do, it is still running with the
configuration it started with.

## Removing it

There is no `disconnect` on the command you have: the verb exists only in
`kaleidoscope`, the manager executable, which is built from source and published
on no channel. So you take the wiring out by hand — the `kaleidoscope` entry in
`~/.claude.json`, the marked block in `CLAUDE.md`, and
`.claude/skills/use-kaleidoscope/` — along with the receipt beside each one,
which is the record of what was put there.
Connect an editor or agent has the whole list in one
place.

---

# Codex

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/codex/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Codex reads the same local engine and the same profile as every other editor you
wire. `kscope init` owns the change it makes to Codex's configuration, marks it,
and leaves a receipt beside it, so you can see exactly what it put there.

## Wire it

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
```

Codex counts as present when `~/.codex` exists. Codex creates that directory
itself, so its presence is evidence rather than a guess, and this command never
creates it on the way to checking.

## What it writes

The MCP entry goes in `~/.codex/config.toml`, inside a block that opens with
`# >>> kaleidoscope-manager owner=kaleidoscope-manager-v1 host=codex` and closes
with the matching `<<<` line. Inside it is an `[mcp_servers.kaleidoscope]` table
naming this executable's absolute path, `args = ["mcp", "--profile", "default"]`,
startup and tool timeouts, and `enabled_tools = ["search", "remember"]` — Codex
is the one editor whose own configuration states the tool list. Everything
outside the block is a textual cut from your original file, so the rest of your
TOML comes back byte for byte, comments and ordering included.

The instruction block goes in `AGENTS.md` in the project, between marker
comments. The skill goes in `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md`, which is
where Codex looks for one — the same path OpenCode reads, and not the one Claude
Code reads.

What gets written does not carry your vault location, a provider key, or an
account credential.

If `~/.codex/config.toml` already contains an `[mcp_servers.kaleidoscope]` table
that Kaleidoscope did not write, the change is refused and nothing is altered.
The command cannot tell where its own text would end and yours begins, and
guessing at that is worse than stopping.

Restart Codex afterwards.

## Removing it

There is no `disconnect` on the command you have: the verb exists only in
`kaleidoscope`, the manager executable, which is built from source and published
on no channel. Removing the wiring is done by hand — the marked block in
`~/.codex/config.toml`, the marked block in `AGENTS.md`, and
`.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/` — with the receipt beside each one.
Connect an editor or agent has the whole list in one
place.

---

# CrewAI

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/crewai/
Updated: 2026-08-30

CrewAI uses one stdio MCP adapter context for the whole crew run, and exposes
only the Kaleidoscope tools you choose to give the model.

## Connect it

```bash
kscope profile launch default
```

`default` there is a profile name, and the profile has to exist before it can
be printed — see profiles and vaults.

Build the adapter from that descriptor, enter it once, select `search` and
`remember`, run the crew, then close the context. Do not recreate the server for
each task.

## What it writes

Nothing on your disk. CrewAI owns your provider configuration and your crew
state; Kaleidoscope owns only the local memory, and never receives a
model-provider credential or an account token.

## Disconnect

Close the adapter context at the end of the crew run and remove the descriptor
from your own configuration.

---

# Cursor

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/cursor/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Cursor uses the same local command and the same two tools as every other editor.
`kscope init` wires it when it can see it, and what it writes for Cursor differs
from every other editor in one way worth knowing about.

## Wire it

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
```

Cursor counts as present when `~/.cursor` exists. Cursor creates that directory
itself; this command does not create it in order to find it.

## What it writes

The MCP server entry goes in `~/.cursor/mcp.json`, under `mcpServers` as
`kaleidoscope`: this executable's absolute path and the arguments
`mcp --profile default`. Entries you added yourself are left untouched, and a
receipt is written beside the file. A tampered marker, a name that conflicts, a
malformed file, a symlink, or a file being edited at the same time is refused
and handed back to you rather than overwritten.

The instructions go in `.cursor/rules/kaleidoscope.mdc` in the project, a rule
file whose frontmatter carries `alwaysApply: true`, so Cursor reads it on every
turn rather than when it happens to look.

The entry carries no vault location, provider key or account credential.

## The one thing that is different here

Cursor is the only one that gets no skill. It has no skill directory to
install one into, so `kscope init` does not attempt it, and the rule file is
the whole of what tells Cursor how to use the memory it can now reach — where
Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode get an instruction file *and* a
`use-kaleidoscope` skill beside it.

That makes the rule the thing to check first. If Cursor can see the tools but
never uses them, it is usually `.cursor/rules/kaleidoscope.mdc` that is missing
or has been edited — see give your agent the skill.

## Removing it

There is no `disconnect` on the command you have: the verb exists only in
`kaleidoscope`, the manager executable, which is built from source and published
on no channel. Take the two pieces out by hand — the `kaleidoscope` entry in
`~/.cursor/mcp.json` and `.cursor/rules/kaleidoscope.mdc` — each with the
receipt written beside it. They were installed independently and they come out
independently, so removing one leaves the other in place.
Connect an editor or agent has the whole list in one
place.

---

# Any other MCP client

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/generic-mcp/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Any standard MCP client can ask Kaleidoscope for its launch descriptor and keep
one initialized session open for the whole run. You do not have to hand-write
the command.

## Get the descriptor

```bash
kscope profile launch default
```

`default` there is a profile name, and the profile has to exist before it can be
printed — see profiles and vaults.

What comes back is deliberately closed: an absolute command,
`mcp --profile NAME`, `stdio`, exactly two tools, and an empty environment. Give
that to your client as its server definition.

## What it writes

Nothing. `kscope init` knows four editors by name — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor
and OpenCode — and wires only those; if it recognises none of them it writes an
`AGENTS.md` and leaves your configuration alone. So you place the descriptor in
your own file, and you own that file. Do not add your vault location or a token
to it.

## The one thing that is different here

One descriptor, one long-lived stdio process. Initialize once, check that you
see exactly `search` and `remember`, then reuse that session for the rest of the
run. Starting a new process per tool call is slower and gains you nothing.

## Disconnect

Remove the server definition from your own configuration. Kaleidoscope wrote
nothing, so there is nothing for it to take back out.

---

# LangChain

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/langchain/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Use the official LangChain MCP adapter to load the two Kaleidoscope tools inside
a single adapter session.

## Connect it

```bash
kscope profile launch default
```

`default` there is a profile name, and the profile has to exist before it can
be printed — see profiles and vaults.

Give that descriptor to the LangChain MCP adapter. Open the stdio adapter once
around the agent run you intend, load the two tools, then close the adapter when
the run is over.

## What it writes

Nothing on your disk. Your model-provider credentials are supplied by your own
application and never pass through Kaleidoscope.

## The one thing that is different here

Kaleidoscope is not a `BaseStore` implementation, and you should not wrap it as
one. Do not add a parallel LangChain memory, and do not summarize messages into
a second store. If two things can answer "what do I know", they will disagree.
The MCP server stays the one owner.

## Disconnect

Close the adapter. Remove the descriptor from your application configuration.

---

# LangGraph

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/langgraph/
Updated: 2026-08-30

LangGraph uses the same one-session MCP adapter as LangChain, placed in your
graph's tool node for the length of the run.

## Connect it

```bash
kscope profile launch default
```

`default` there is a profile name, and the profile has to exist before it can
be printed — see profiles and vaults.

Open the adapter before you execute the graph, pass the two tools into the tool
node, and close it once execution finishes. The same session is reused across
node calls.

## What it writes

Nothing on your disk. Provider credentials stay in your own application.

## The one thing that is different here

Kaleidoscope is not a LangGraph checkpointer and not a `BaseStore`. Keep graph
state and durable memory separate, so you never end up with two things that both
claim to be the record.

## Disconnect

Close the adapter after the graph finishes, and remove the descriptor from your
own configuration.

---

# OpenAI Agents SDK

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/openai-agents-sdk/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Use the stdio MCP server lifecycle the OpenAI Agents SDK already gives you. Keep
one server alive for the agent run, and filter the model-facing tools down to
Kaleidoscope's two.

## Connect it

```bash
kscope profile launch default
```

`default` there is a profile name, and the profile has to exist before it can
be printed — see profiles and vaults.

Create the MCP server from that descriptor as a managed resource around the run,
and close it deterministically at the end. Do not open a fresh engine process
for every tool call.

## What it writes

Nothing on your disk. Provider credentials come from your application and are
never placed in the Kaleidoscope descriptor.

## The one thing that is different here

The tool allowlist is two names, `search` and `remember`. Nothing else is ever
exposed to a model — the operator commands are yours, from the terminal.

## Disconnect

Close the server at the end of the run and remove the descriptor from your own
configuration.

# OpenCode

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/integrations/opencode/
Updated: 2026-08-30

OpenCode stable v1 and beta v2 want different configuration shapes. Kaleidoscope
never guesses which one you are on and never quietly moves you between them.

## Wire it

```bash
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
```

OpenCode counts as present when `~/.config/opencode` or `~/.opencode` exists.
OpenCode creates those itself; this command does not create one in order to find
it.

## What it writes

The MCP entry goes in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`. In the stable v1
shape that is `mcp.kaleidoscope`, with `"type": "local"`, `"enabled": true`, and
a `command` array holding this executable's absolute path followed by `mcp`,
`--profile` and `default`. Only that entry is written; the rest of the file
comes back as it was, and a receipt is left beside it.

The instruction block goes in `AGENTS.md` in the project, and the skill in
`.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md` — the same two paths Codex reads,
because OpenCode reads them too.

The entry carries no vault location, provider key or account credential.

## The one thing that is different here

Which of the two shapes you get is read off your file rather than chosen for
you. An `opencode.json` with no Kaleidoscope entry gets stable v1. One that
already has an `mcp.servers` object — the beta v2 container — gets beta v2
instead: the entry goes to `mcp.servers.kaleidoscope` and carries
`"codemode": false`, so `search` and `remember` stay visible to the model as
tools. If both shapes are present, or the shape in your file conflicts with the
one Kaleidoscope already owns, the change is refused and handed back for you to
resolve.

The command you have takes no flag for this. `--opencode-version` belongs to
`kaleidoscope`, the manager executable, which is built from source and published
on no channel; on `kscope` the shape follows the file.

## Removing it

There is no `disconnect` on the command you have either. Take the wiring out by
hand — the `kaleidoscope` entry in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`, the
marked block in `AGENTS.md`, and `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/` — with the
receipt beside each one, which is the record of what was put there.
Connect an editor or agent has the whole list in one
place.

---

# Licenses and product terms

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/legal/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Reviewed drafts — not yet in force.
The product terms below have been reviewed by legal counsel for Kleos Research Private Limited. Apache-2.0 and CC BY 4.0 are authorized license selections and are in force for the material they cover. The engine EULA, privacy notice, security policy, and support policy have been reviewed but have not yet been adopted: they are not in force, are not offers or contracts, and do not describe terms that govern anything today. They will take effect when the company formally adopts them.

The public software, original documentation, and proprietary engine have
deliberately separate license boundaries. Two of them are settled; the rest are
drafts.

## Authorized public licenses

**Apache-2.0 — in force.** Covers the public manager, SDKs, wrappers,
integrations, and skill, and is carried in those source and package
repositories. It does not license the native engine, model weights, trademarks,
or third-party material.

**CC BY 4.0 — in force.** Covers original documentation. Read the
documentation license scope and the
CC BY 4.0 legal code.

## Product terms — review drafts

| document | plain text |
|---|---|
| Proprietary engine EULA | `ENGINE-EULA.txt` |
| Privacy notice | `PRIVACY-NOTICE.txt` |
| Security policy | `SECURITY-POLICY.txt` |
| Support policy | `SUPPORT-POLICY.txt` |

## What is still outstanding

- **External legal review.** No lawyer has read any of these documents. This is
  the gate that keeps every draft above out of force, and it is now the only one
  of its kind: the drafts are complete rather than partial, so what is left is
  review and a decision to adopt, not missing terms.
- **A compliance question inside them.** The drafts identify the contracting
  party by name, company type, place of registration, and contact address, and
  undertake to supply the registered office address and Corporate Identity
  Number to anyone who asks. Two provisions bear on that and the reviewer has to
  decide both. Section 12(3)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires the name,
  registered office address and CIN in a company's business letters, billheads,
  letter papers "and in all its notices and other official publications" —
  whether published product terms are an "official publication" is arguable.
  Rule 26(1) of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014, as substituted with
  effect from 27 July 2016, is the more direct one: it requires a company with a
  website to publish its name, registered office address, CIN, telephone number,
  email and a contact for queries or grievances **on the landing or home page**.
  Both values are already public on the MCA portal against the company name, so
  the question is compliance form rather than confidentiality.
- **Third-party notices.** The embedding model inside the engine is Kleos
  Research's own work and carries no third-party attribution. The open-source
  libraries linked into the engine are a separate question, and they are not yet
  enumerated in the EULA or in the engine's own output. That has to be finished
  before a release.
- **Commitments.** Support scope is deliberately best effort with no response
  time, and no service level exists. That is a decision, not a gap.

# MCP reference

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/mcp/
Release: 0.0.5
Updated: 2026-08-30

Your editor or agent sees exactly two tools from Kaleidoscope: `search` and
`remember`. Nothing else is callable by a model. This page is what you need to
write a correct call to either one.

To connect a host of your own you need the package and a key — see
Install — and then `kscope init` in the project, which
registers the server with every editor and agent it finds. The contract below is
the one that runs locally, against the vault that command created.

Read the machine-readable tool reference.

## `search`

Send exactly one of `query` or `memory_id`. A `query` ranks your memories and
returns them under `selected_hits`. A `memory_id` is an addressed read: it
returns that one memory at the top level and refuses ranking controls. Keep
`top_k` small — about 5 is normal — and set a bounded `maximum_context_bytes`.
`ledger` accepts only `true`.

```json
{"query": "how do we handle database migrations", "top_k": 5, "ledger": true}
```

A query also writes down what it returned. That record goes into your vault on
your machine, next to the memories themselves, and it stays there — it is what a
later authenticated tool would use to tell which memories actually helped.

## `remember`

`mode` is required and is `create`, `update`, or `delete`. For a create or an
update, `content_md` is the memory as you want to read it back and must begin
with an H1, and `semantic_delta` carries the structure: a title and at least one
fact. Every endpoint a fact names is declared with `n`, the surface the fact
refers to it by; `kind`; and `is`, a short gloss. Predicates are snake_case. An
update or a delete needs `memory_id` and `expected_version_id`. Batching through
`items` accepts at most 20 creates, and items do not share structure with each
other.

```json
{
  "mode": "create",
  "content_md": "# Ana owns the billing service\n\nAna took it over after the payments team split.",
  "semantic_delta": {
    "memory_type": "decision",
    "title": "Ana owns the billing service",
    "entities": [
      {"n": "Ana", "kind": "person", "is": "backend engineer on my team"},
      {"n": "billing service", "kind": "service", "is": "the service that issues invoices"}
    ],
    "facts": [{"subject": "Ana", "predicate": "owns", "object": "billing service"}]
  }
}
```

Write the `is` gloss properly. It is not documentation — it is what the engine
matches on when it decides whether two mentions of a name are the same thing, so
`Ana | person | backend engineer on my team` finds far more than `Ana` alone
does.

`remember` infers nothing from what you wrote. The entities, facts,
relationships, and dates it stores are the ones you state explicitly. Treat the
tool schema your host discovered as the authority for which memory types and
fields a build accepts, rather than copying a vocabulary out of prose.

## Lifecycle

Your host keeps one long-lived process alive across calls and talks to it over
stdio at MCP protocol revision `2025-11-25`. It negotiates once, enforces a
startup deadline, cancels cleanly, bounds what it reads from stderr, and shuts
the process down without leaving an orphan behind. A framework integration will
not run a second retrieval behind your back.

## What a model never sees

Feedback, lifecycle and import, maintenance, ontology, and diagnostics are
operator commands, not tools. They are absent from the list your agent
discovers. Search results do not carry the handle those commands need either, so
there is no path from a model to them and nothing to reconstruct.

## Telling your agent to use them

Discovering the two tools is not the same as using them well. The skill file
that tells an agent when to retrieve and what is worth writing is published at
give your agent the skill.

---

# Operations

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/operations/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Your memory lives in one place on your machine — a vault directory you chose.
Everything else Kaleidoscope touches (editor configuration, agent instructions,
account credentials, the installed executables) has its own lifecycle, and
removing any of them does not remove your memory.

## Find your profile first

You named a vault root when you initialized a profile. To see which profile is
active and where it points, without printing credentials or any memory content:

```bash
kscope profile list
kscope where
echo '{"mode":"inspect"}' | kscope call --profile default doctor
```

`where` answers the narrower question: which vault a command that names none
would resolve to from here, and where that answer came from. `doctor` in
`inspect` mode reads health and writes nothing, and what it prints on stdout is
counts and status fields — no memory content and no absolute paths. The line
beside it on stderr is not part of that report: it names the resolved vault, by
absolute path.

## Back up and restore

Back up by copying the whole vault directory while nothing is connected to it —
close the editors and agents you have connected first, so nothing is writing to
it mid-copy. Copy the directory as a whole; a partial copy is not a vault. To
restore, or to move your memory to another machine or another path, put the
directory back and point a profile at it:

```bash
kscope profile import restored /absolute/path/to/the/vault
```

`profile import` reads the vault's own identity out of the vault and writes a
profile pointing at it. It creates no vault and moves no canonical data, which
is why it is the command for a directory you have put back rather than `init`,
which will not initialise over a root that is already a vault: it leaves that
directory exactly as it is and tells you so.

## Disconnect and uninstall

These are four separate operations, and it matters that you know which one you
are doing.

- Removing an editor's connection means removing the Kaleidoscope entry from
  that editor's configuration. `kscope init` wrote that entry and left a receipt
  marking it as its own, so it is clear which block is yours to delete and which
  settings in the same file to leave alone. There is no shipped command that
  does the removal for you: `disconnect` and `teardown` are verbs of the
  separate manager executable, which is published on no channel.
- Removing the agent guidance — the instruction file and the skill that `init`
  installed — is a separate act from removing the connection, and today it is
  also done by hand.
- Uninstalling the package removes the executables:
  `npm uninstall -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope`.
- Removing account credentials would be the fourth. There is nothing to remove
  today: there is no account to sign in to, and the commands that would sign you
  out are in the unpublished manager.

None of the four deletes a vault. Your memory survives all of them.

## Delete a vault

Deleting a vault is deliberately its own operation: it previews what it will
delete, asks you to confirm, and acts on exactly one fully resolved path. A
broad path, an unresolved variable, or an ambiguous target is refused rather
than guessed at. Deleting a memory and deleting the vault that holds it are
different acts — the first is something you ask the engine to do, the second
removes the files.

## Install, update, and roll back

Installing, updating, rolling back to the previous version, and uninstalling
have each been run on a Mac with Apple Silicon and behaved correctly, and a
vault kept alongside was byte-for-byte identical afterwards. That is the whole
of what has been established. npm is the channel, and naming a version —
`npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope@` — is how you pin one and
how you go back to one. Nothing is signed for production, and the sequence above
has been run once, on one machine, so read it as a mechanism we have tried
rather than a supported update path.

## What gets installed

Two things: the npm package `@kleos-research/kaleidoscope`, and a second package
built for your platform. The npm package holds the client library and the
`kscope` command; the platform package holds one program — the engine as object
code, with the setup half of the manager compiled into it. There is no install
hook, runtime download, compiler, or source-build fallback — nothing is fetched
or built on your machine after the download. The engine source is not in the
package. There is no Python package to install: `kscope-memory` on PyPI is a
0.0.0 placeholder, and nothing else of ours is registered there.

## Encrypted vaults, on a Mac

On a Mac you can choose to keep a vault inside an encrypted disk image. Its
password is generated by macOS, kept in your login Keychain, and shown to you
once as a recovery key — write that down, it is the only copy. This is macOS
only; elsewhere the command refuses.

---

# Install

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/packages/
Release: 0.0.5
Updated: 2026-08-30

```bash
npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope
```

That is the whole install. You need a key to run it — email
contact@kleosresearch.xyz and we will send
you one.

## What your machine needs

| | |
|---|---|
| operating system | macOS or Linux |
| architecture | arm64 (Apple Silicon) or x86_64 |
| Node.js | 18 or newer |

Windows is not supported yet. No Windows package is published, so there is no
executable for the install to bring down, and creating a vault is refused in the
code as well until the filesystem work is done.

There is no Python package you can use. `kscope-memory` on PyPI is registered,
but only as a 0.0.0 placeholder whose own summary says "Local memory for AI
agents. Not yet released." — installing it gets you nothing.
`kaleidoscope-memory` was planned and never registered; if you find that name,
it is not us.

## What it puts on your disk

Two things. The first is the `kscope` command and a small amount of JavaScript
that picks the right binary for your machine. The second is a package built for
your platform, which carries the part that stores and searches your memory.

There is no install hook, no download at install time, no compiler step and no
source-build fallback. Installing puts files on your disk and does nothing else.

The part that stores and searches your memory is proprietary object code, and
its source is not in the package. A native binary is still inspectable —
shipping object code is not a claim that it cannot be read. Everything around
it is Apache-2.0: the command-line tool, both SDKs, every integration and the
agent skill.

## Signing

Nothing is signed for release. There is no Apple signing and no notarisation,
and the native code is ad-hoc signed only. That is worth knowing before you
install, and it is on the list to fix.

What works today · Which platforms this is for
