# Privacy and data boundary

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/privacy/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Your memory and your account identity are separate systems. Signing in does not
authorize upload, sync, analysis, training on, or deletion of your memory.

## Your memory stays local

Signing in never carries your memory with it. Memory content, the queries you
ran, the results you got back, memory IDs, graph data, local paths, vault
locations, the internal identifiers Kaleidoscope uses to organise a vault, and
any credentials you have stored locally are all excluded from the account
protocol. The account client rejects those fields — and any absolute local path
— before anything would leave your machine.

## What signing in would send

Signing in would send a narrow set of account and device fields — enough to log
in, keep you logged in, show your account status, link or unlink another sign-in
provider, log out, and manage the devices attached to your account. Nothing
else. You cannot sign in today, and the terms that would govern it — who runs
the sign-in service, how long anything is kept, how you recover an account, and
how you delete one — are not settled. That is one of the reasons sign-in is
switched off.

## Where a sign-in credential would be kept

Signing in is not built yet, so nothing is stored anywhere today. When it is,
the refresh credential goes to the operating system's own credential store — the
login Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows, the Secret Service on
Linux — and never into a file we write, into an editor's configuration, or into
a profile. On Linux, if no secret service is running, signing in stops and tells
you rather than falling back to something weaker.

There is a caveat about unsigned software and macOS credential prompts, and one
about alpha keys, which do not use a credential store at all. Both are on
Account and devices.

## Network use

The part that stores and searches your memory needs no network access and makes
no calls to any model provider. Storing, searching and reading your memory all
work with your machine offline.

One thing does reach the network: checking that your key is still valid. That
check sends three things — your key, the platform you are running on, and the
version of the component that makes the check. Nothing else goes with it: no memory
content, no queries, no results, no file paths. The key travels in the
request's authorization header, and the body is those other two fields and no
more. A test in the engine holds the body to exactly those two fields and fails
if anything about your memory is added to it. That test is the positive half:
it proves what this build sends, and the enforcement that a future build cannot
quietly send more lives in the service that receives it. The check runs in the background and caches its
answer, so it is not on the path of anything you do.

There is no account to create and no sign-in.

## This documentation site

These pages are static files served by GitHub Pages. They set no cookies. They do
keep two things in your own browser, both functional and neither sent anywhere:
your light-or-dark theme choice, in local storage, and the navigation sidebar's
state — which groups you left open, where you had scrolled, and a short check
value — in session storage, which your browser discards when you close the tab. The only scripts on them are the small ones that make the
navigation work; there is no analytics, no behavioural tracking, and nothing
that reports your reading anywhere. They do make one
third-party request: the three typefaces are fetched from Google Fonts
(`fonts.googleapis.com` and `fonts.gstatic.com`), so Google receives the request
metadata a font fetch carries, including your IP address. Blocking it costs only
the typefaces. Nothing on this site reads a vault, a profile, or any local
memory.

## Hosted memory

There is no hosted service. Kaleidoscope does not sync your memory anywhere,
there is no endpoint or API to send it to, and there is no waitlist for one. If
that ever changes it will be a separate product with its own terms, and it will
not be something a local profile or a sign-in quietly opts you into.

---

The current version is 0.0.5. It was published to npm as

platforms it is built for — macOS on Apple Silicon and x86_64, Linux on arm64
and x86_64. It gives you the `kscope` command, it needs a key to run, and
nothing in it is signed for release. Install is how you get

There is no entry below for it, and none for the versions before it. Notes begin
with the next version, and from there every version will be listed here, newest
first.

Each entry will say which platforms that version runs on, which editor and agent
versions it was checked against, what changed, what broke or was removed, whether
anything you already have needs to be moved or reconfigured, and any security

# Security

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/security/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Kaleidoscope's engine is distributed as object code rather than source. That is
a distribution choice, not a security guarantee: a native binary on your machine
is still inspectable and may be reverse engineered, and shipping object code is
not a claim of impossibility. What this page describes is the boundaries you can
check — what the engine can reach, what account commands can send, and what is
not signed.

## What the engine can reach

The engine keeps your memory in a local vault, speaks stdio to your editor,
declares no required network access, and makes no external model calls. When the
manager launches it, it hands over a closed, non-secret environment rather than
passing along whatever is in yours — your model-provider keys, account tokens,
cloud credentials and the vault's location are not part of what the engine
process receives.

## What account commands can send

Account commands never touch the memory engine. The manager can reach exactly
eleven account routes and no others, and a guard rejects memory and profile
fields, and absolute local paths, before anything is sent. With the engine
deliberately removed from the machine, all eleven still refused cleanly with
`provider not configured` — they fail before anything local is opened. There is
no account service to reach in any case.

## Nothing is signed for production

There is no Apple signing and no notarisation. The only signature that exists
anywhere in the build is a test fixture checked into the source, and the native
code is ad-hoc signed only. Do not read any of this as a supply-chain guarantee:
nothing here lets you verify that a file you received is the file we built.
Production trust roots, signing identities and the final notices that go with
them do not exist yet.

This has a consequence you will meet before any other: an unsigned program has
no stable identity for the operating system to remember, so a macOS credential
prompt can come back every launch. That is the reason the
account page says a
Keychain approval may not stick.

## What we have checked for leaks

We put distinctive marker values into the environment, the profiles, the editor
configuration and the MCP traffic, then check that none of them turn up in
output. That is a scoped test on one platform, not a proof that nothing ever
leaks — it can only find the kinds of leak it was written to look for.

## Report a vulnerability

Do not publish an exploit or a sensitive report in a public issue. There is no
security contact to send it to yet; publishing one, along with a policy saying
which versions get fixes, is something that has to happen before release. It
will appear on this page and at `/.well-known/security.txt`.

---

# Give your agent the skill

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/skill/
Updated: 2026-08-30

An agent only uses memory if something told it to. Kaleidoscope ships one skill
file and a short pointer for whichever instruction file your project already has,
and it installs them as a block it owns, so what it wrote can always be told
apart from what you wrote.

Installing the package writes none of it, and neither does running the memory
server. `kscope init` writes it, it is a command a person runs, it says on your
screen what it did, and `kscope init --no-wire` is how you tell it to create the
vault and leave every file of yours alone. That flag works and is absent from
the binary's own `--help`, which is worth knowing before you go looking for it
there.

## The four files

Every one is published here, byte for byte, as `kscope init` installs it.

They are copies, and the thing that makes the claim checkable is that they are
copies of something named. The originals are
`crates/kaleidoscope-manager/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md` and
`crates/kaleidoscope-manager/snippets/` in the product source, compiled into the
executable, so the bytes `kscope init` writes are those and no others.
`/site-manifest.json` records, for each of the four, the
sha256 of the source it was taken from, under `public_upstream_sha256`, and the
build refuses to publish a copy that no longer matches its digest. The digests
live in that file rather than in this sentence because a digest is something to
check with, not something to read: download a file below, take its sha256, and
compare. This page has been wrong about these bytes before, and a claim that
nothing re-checks is how that happened.

SKILL.md — https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/SKILL.md

The skill itself — about 1,500 words telling an agent how to use `search` and
`remember`, when to retrieve, what is worth persisting, and what never to store.
Claude Code reads it at `.claude/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md`; Codex and
OpenCode read `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md`. It is the same file
either way.

AGENTS.md snippet — https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/snippets/AGENTS.md

The marked block for your project's `AGENTS.md`, which Codex and OpenCode read.
It points at the skill and states the rules in short, so an agent that never
opens the skill still has them.

CLAUDE.md snippet — https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/snippets/CLAUDE.md

The same block for `CLAUDE.md`, differing where it must: it names the skill path
Claude Code reads, which is not the one `AGENTS.md` names.

Cursor rule — https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/snippets/cursor-kaleidoscope.mdc

The same block as a Cursor project rule, with `alwaysApply: true`. It names no
skill file, because Cursor has no skill directory to read one from, and points
at `kscope schema remember` for the write contract instead.

## What gets added to your file

The two comments are the point: they mark where Kaleidoscope's text starts and
stops.

````md title="CLAUDE.md" wrap
<!-- >>> kaleidoscope-manager owner=kaleidoscope-manager-v1 instruction=claude -->
## Kaleidoscope memory

This project's memory across sessions: decisions made, preferences stated, constraints, corrections, and what past work produced. `search` reads it, `remember` writes it. All local -- no network, nothing leaves this machine.

**Prefer the CLI when you have a shell.** One invocation costs a couple of dozen tokens; the MCP tool definitions sit in your context all session (~1,800) whether or not you call them. Use the MCP `search`/`remember` tools only when you have no shell -- same engine, same vault.

```bash
echo '{"query":"how we handle retries","top_k":5}' | kscope call --profile default search
kscope schema remember   # the write contract, when you need it
```

**Search before you go looking.** Before grepping, reading your way around the code, or asking the user how this project works -- search first. Code shows what *is*; memory shows what was *decided*, and why. A question already settled here must not be asked twice.

**Write without being asked** when the user states a preference, makes or rejects a decision, sets a constraint, corrects you, or work produces a result worth keeping. Don't wait for "remember this", and don't batch writes to the end of the task -- write when it lands, while you still know why.

**Write what you had to dig for.** Those triggers are things the *user* did; this one is you. Whatever you established by reading code, running an experiment, or ruling out a wrong answer is the most expensive thing in a session to rediscover. **That applies hardest to agents you spawn.** A subagent or workflow agent sees only the prompt you write it, so put "search Kaleidoscope first, record what you establish" in that prompt -- or write its findings yourself when it reports back.

Never store secrets, transcripts, ordinary file contents, anything the code or git history already records, or ideas still in flux.

A refusal names the field to fix and what to change it to: correct it and resend. One refusal is never a reason to stop using memory.

Full write contract: `.claude/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md`, or `kscope schema remember`.
<!-- <<< kaleidoscope-manager owner=kaleidoscope-manager-v1 instruction=claude -->
````

The middle is elided on purpose. The block is about a page long, and a second
copy of it living in this page's source is precisely what drifted the last time:
the file offered above is the text, and it is the one checked against the
source. [Read it in full](/snippets/CLAUDE.md).

Nothing else in your file is touched, and nothing is added a second time if you
run it twice.

## Where each file lands

The skill directory is not the same for every agent, and a skill file written to
the wrong one is a file that is silently never loaded. `kscope init` writes the
path the agent in front of it actually reads.

| what | lands at | form |
|---|---|---|
| the skill, for Claude Code | `.claude/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md` | the whole file |
| the skill, for Codex and OpenCode | `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md` | the whole file |
| the block, for Claude Code | `CLAUDE.md` in the project | one marked block, appended |
| the block, for Codex and OpenCode | `AGENTS.md` in the project | one marked block, appended |
| the rule, for Cursor | `.cursor/rules/kaleidoscope.mdc` | the whole file, with frontmatter |

Cursor has no skill row because it has no skill directory: asking for one there
is refused rather than written somewhere it would not be read. All five paths are
inside the project, which is what carries them into the worktree or the
temporary clone an agent usually runs your work in.

In `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` the block is delimited by an HTML comment pair. In
the Cursor rule the file *is* Kaleidoscope's, so the pair wraps the whole of it:
the opening marker sits in the frontmatter as a `#` comment and the closing
marker is the last line. `SKILL.md` carries no marker anywhere — its frontmatter
is `name` and `description` and nothing else — because a skill file is parsed by
the agent that loads it, and a comment injected into that frontmatter is a file a
strict reader can reject outright. What records ownership there is a receipt
written beside it, `.kaleidoscope-instruction-owner.json`. Marker or receipt, the
job is the same: it is what makes a second install idempotent instead of
duplicating, what makes an exact removal possible, and what is read before a file
is touched at all.

Those writes are bounded on purpose. Each is atomic and leaves a bounded backup
beside the file; unrelated content is left alone; running it again changes
nothing; and a target that is unknown, conflicting, symlinked, hand-edited inside
the markers, or changed underneath it is refused, not overwritten. A refusal
costs you that one file and nothing else — a Cursor rule that cannot be written
does not cost you your Claude Code registration — and none of it can undo the
vault, which exists before any of this runs.

Two things you may have read elsewhere are not on the command that ships. There
is no preview-then-confirm step: `kscope init` applies as it goes and names each
step as it takes it. And there is no removal command; taking the text back out is
done by hand, by deleting the marked block including both of its comments, or the
skill file and the receipt beside it.

## Installing them

`kscope init` writes all of it, in the same run that creates the vault. It needs
a key to run at all — [getting started](/docs/getting-started/) says how to ask
for one.

```bash
npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope
cd ~/your-project
kscope init
```

It looks for the configuration directory each agent creates in your home
directory — `~/.claude` or `~/.claude.json`, `~/.codex`, `~/.cursor`,
`~/.config/opencode` — and treats its existence as evidence that you run that
agent, rather than guessing. For each one it finds it registers the memory
server, writes the instruction file and installs the skill, printing a line per
step. When it finds none it writes `AGENTS.md` alone and says that is what it
did, because `AGENTS.md` is the one file every agent reads.

## Doing it by hand

If you ran `kscope init --no-wire`, or you use an agent this build has never
heard of, the files above are the whole mechanism and pasting them works:

1. Save `SKILL.md` to `.claude/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md` for Claude Code,
   or `.agents/skills/use-kaleidoscope/SKILL.md` for Codex or OpenCode.
2. Paste the matching snippet into `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, or
   `.cursor/rules/kaleidoscope.mdc` — **keep the two marker comments**. They are
   what lets Kaleidoscope recognise the block as its own later, and remove it
   exactly, instead of treating it as your own text and refusing to touch it.

## The commands of the other program

`kaleidoscope instructions install` writes one of these files at a time, and
`instructions remove` takes one back out exactly. They belong to `kaleidoscope`,
a second executable that is built only from the product source and published on
no channel: you cannot obtain it, so you cannot run any of the lines below today.
They are written down because that finer-grained half of the mechanism is real
and is where this is going, not because there is a way to reach it.

```bash
kaleidoscope instructions install skill  --host claude-code --project "$PWD"
kaleidoscope instructions install agents --project "$PWD" --dry-run
kaleidoscope instructions install agents --project "$PWD"
kaleidoscope instructions install claude --project "$PWD"
kaleidoscope instructions install cursor --project "$PWD"

kaleidoscope instructions remove cursor --project "$PWD" --dry-run
kaleidoscope instructions remove cursor --project "$PWD"
```

`install skill` requires `--host`, because the skill directory differs per agent
and there is no sensible default to pick; the other three targets take no such
flag. `--dry-run` prints the plan and changes nothing. Without `--yes` you are
asked to confirm. `instructions remove` is the exact inverse of
`instructions install`: it takes out the marked block and leaves the rest of the
file as it was. If you edited inside the markers, it stops and hands the file
back rather than overwriting your work.

Full command reference: the instructions commands.
What the two tools actually do: MCP reference.
The same text as a single file: agent-instructions.md.

---

# Troubleshooting

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/docs/troubleshooting/
Updated: 2026-08-30

Start with `kscope where` when your profile, engine, or host configuration is
misbehaving: it prints the vault a command that names none would resolve to from
here, and where that answer came from. It needs no key, which is why it is the
first thing to try. The fuller check is
`echo '' | kscope call doctor`, which reads health and writes
nothing — but `call` is one of the commands the key gates, so a refusal there is
about your key rather than about your vault. Signing in sits on its own separate
boundary and is not a local failure at all, so read that section below before
you conclude anything here is broken.

## The host cannot find the tools

1. Confirm the active profile is the one you expect, with `kscope profile list`
   and `kscope where`.
2. Open the host's own configuration file and read only the block Kaleidoscope
   owns — `kscope init` marks the entry it wrote as its own, so which block that
   is does not have to be guessed.
3. Restart the host after `kscope init` — most hosts read their configuration
   once, at startup.
4. Confirm the tools it discovered are exactly `search` and `remember`.

## OpenCode configuration is refused

The stable and beta-v2 configuration shapes differ. Kaleidoscope adopts an
existing shape when it is unambiguous, or the version you named explicitly; it
never quietly rewrites stable configuration into beta. Remove any duplicate
Kaleidoscope entry and run `kscope init` again.

## A profile points to the wrong place

Do not edit the profile by hand. `kscope profile import NAME ROOT` reads the
identity out of the vault you meant to use and writes a profile pointing at it;
`kscope init ROOT RFC3339_CREATED_AT` makes a new vault at an explicit path, and
that second argument is a timestamp — `2026-08-30T09:00:00Z` — not a name. A
missing or invalid root is refused rather than created for you, so nothing is
silently written to the wrong place.

## You cannot sign in

There is nothing to sign in to, and what you installed does not try. `kscope`
carries no login, logout, or account command at all — those are verbs of a
separate `kaleidoscope` manager executable that is published on no channel, so
they are commands you cannot obtain rather than commands that fail. Your key is
what entitles the machine, and `kscope activate` is how it gets there. Do not
delete or recreate your vault over this: your account status and your local
memory were never connected, and you do not need an account to use your memory.

## The install did not work

The install is `npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope`, and npm picks the
platform package for your machine out of the four that are published — macOS on
Apple Silicon and x86_64, Linux on arm64 and x86_64. On Windows there is no
package to bring down, so the install has nothing to give you.

If `kscope` installed but refuses to run, the key is a likelier cause than the
download. `kscope gate` prints what this build gates and the path it reads a key
from, without reading the key or opening a vault, and `kscope activate` is what
puts the key there. Nothing is signed for release either, so an operating-system
refusal to launch an unsigned binary is about the missing signature and not a
corrupt install.

## The agent can see the tools but never uses them

Discovering `search` and `remember` is not the same as being told to use them.
Install the skill and the pointer block for your project:
give your agent the skill.

## Before sharing diagnostics

Strip local paths, account identifiers, provider keys, tokens, memory content,
queries, results, and vault locations before you send anything to anyone. Use
what `kscope call doctor` prints on stdout in `inspect` mode, which is the
artifact meant for that: counts and status fields, and no memory content or
absolute paths. The line it writes to stderr beside it is not part of that — it
names the vault it resolved, by absolute path.

---

# Status

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/status/
Release: 0.0.5
Updated: 2026-08-30

As of 2026-08-30

Kaleidoscope is installable and needs a key to run. Nothing is signed for
release, and there is no account to sign in to. That is the whole status, and
the rest of this page says what each part of it means.

## Is anything down?

No, and there is nothing that could be.

Kaleidoscope runs on your machine. The engine that stores and ranks your memory
is a local process; there is no server between you and it, no API endpoint, no
hosted memory, and no account service you depend on to read your own vault. A
status page for a local program has no uptime to report, and we would rather say
that than invent a green tick.

If a hosted service ever exists, its status will be published here, and this
section will say something other than "there is nothing that could be down."

## Can I install it?

Yes.

```bash
npm install -g @kleos-research/kaleidoscope
```

macOS and Linux, on Apple Silicon and x86_64. Windows is not supported yet.

You need a key to run it — email
contact@kleosresearch.xyz. There is no
Python package you can use: `kscope-memory` is registered on PyPI, but only as a
0.0.0 placeholder that ships no working code and says as much in its own
summary, and `kaleidoscope-memory` was planned and never registered.

Nothing is signed for release, so what you install is unsigned software on your
machine. That is on the list to fix.

## Do I need an account?

No, and there is no way to make one. Your key is all that is needed, and your
vault has never depended on an account.

## What version is current

| | |
|---|---|
| Package | 0.0.5 on npm |
| Documentation | updated 2026-08-30 |
| Signed builds | none |

## Two contracts you can check right now

They are published as files, and they are the closest thing to a live interface
this project has today:

- The two tools a model sees — `search` and
  `remember`, and nothing else. No operator command is ever a model tool.
- The full command-line help — every command and
  flag of `kscope`, verbatim. It is the help text of the one program that
  installs: there is no second executable to install, so a command it does not
  name is one no download of ours gives you. It is a page about commands rather
  than a complete inventory of behaviour — `--no-wire`, for one, works and is
  not on it.

## What we have actually run

This is the part that is easy to overstate, so it is stated flatly.

**Machines.** Kaleidoscope has been run on one kind of machine: a Mac with Apple
Silicon. It is built and published for four — macOS on Apple Silicon and x86_64,
Linux on arm64 and x86_64 — so on any of them there is something to install. A
build existing for a platform is not the same as our having run it there, and on
the other three we have not, which is what this section is for. Windows on x86_64 has had a compiler check of the
memory engine's source and nothing more: nothing was assembled into a program for
it, nothing was linked, and nothing has been run there.

**Editors and agents.** From the command line, on that Mac:

- Codex 0.149.0 — what happened: Kaleidoscope's entry is added to Codex's configuration, listed, read back and removed exactly, leaving the file byte for byte as it was. What did not: that Codex then starts the server and sees the two tools; Codex's command line offers no way to check.
- Claude Code 2.1.239 — what happened: connected from the command line, not duplicated on a second run, removed cleanly, and both tools discovered. What did not: any run through a model turn, and anything done through the graphical interface.
- OpenCode 1.18.21 — what happened: both configuration shapes written, applied twice without duplicating, removed cleanly, and both tools discovered. What did not: any run through a model turn, and anything done through the graphical interface.
- Cursor — what happened: its configuration and its project rule are written and removed exactly. What did not: everything after that; Cursor has never been launched against them.

      what happenedwhat did not

**Frameworks.** LangChain, LangGraph, the Claude Agent SDK, the OpenAI Agents SDK
and CrewAI have been run against stand-in models, never a live provider.

**Not done at all:** any run against a live model provider, anything through an
editor's graphical interface, any platform other than a Mac with Apple Silicon,
and any package installed from a registry.

The same facts, in machine-readable form: status.json for the
status above, and platform-support.json for the
platform matrix, which is stated there and nowhere else.

# Public agent skill

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/SKILL.md

---
name: use-kaleidoscope
description: Kaleidoscope is the user's local memory for this project — the decisions, preferences, constraints and outcomes a new session would otherwise have to rediscover or ask about twice. Use this skill at the start of any nontrivial task; before you grep the codebase or ask the user how something works; whenever the user states a preference, makes a decision, sets a constraint, or corrects you; when a piece of work produces a result worth keeping; and whenever the user says remember, save, note, forget or "what did we decide". Use it too when a Kaleidoscope call is refused, or when you cannot find its tools — it says what to do instead of quietly working without memory.
---

# Use Kaleidoscope

Kaleidoscope remembers things about *this project* so you do not have to work
them out again: what was decided and why, what the user prefers, what has
already been tried and rejected, what a past piece of work actually produced.

Two things you can do. **Read it** with `search`. **Write to it** with
`remember`. That is the whole surface.

Everything is local. No network call, nothing leaves this machine.

## How to call it

**If you have a shell, use the CLI.** It is much the cheaper route — one
command costs a couple of dozen tokens, while the MCP tool definitions sit in
your context all session whether you use them or not.

```bash
# read
echo '{"query":"why we chose this database","top_k":5}' | kscope call --profile default search

# the write contract, whenever you need it
kscope schema remember
```

If your harness gives you `search` and `remember` as tools and you have no
shell, use those instead. Same engine, same vault, same answers. Your harness
may show them under a prefix — Claude Code prefixes every tool with its server
— so use whatever name your own tool list shows.

## Reading: search first, then go looking

**Before you grep, before you read your way around the codebase, and before you
ask the user how something works — search.**

That includes: why is this built this way, what did we decide about X, what does
the user prefer, what did we already try. The code tells you what *is*.
Kaleidoscope tells you what was *decided*, and why — which the code cannot.

Ask for what you actually need, in plain words:

```bash
echo '{"query":"retry and backoff policy for the payments client","top_k":5}' \
  | kscope call --profile default search
```

One search at the start of a task is usually enough. Search again if the goal
changes, if something you read contradicts it, or if what came back was clearly
stale.

Treat what you get back as good context, not as gospel. If a memory disagrees
with what the user is telling you right now, **the user wins** — and that
disagreement is itself worth writing down.

And the point of all this: **a question already answered here is one you must
not ask the user a second time.**

## Writing: save it when it happens

Call `remember` without being asked. The moments that matter:

- the user states a preference — *"always use X"*, *"never do Y"*
- a decision gets made or rejected
- the user sets a constraint — a budget, a deadline, a rule
- the user corrects something you did or said
- a piece of work produces a result worth keeping
- **you worked something out** — see below

"Remember this", "save this" and "note that" are obvious triggers, but do not
wait for them. And **do not save everything up for the end of the task** — write
when the decision lands, while you still know why it was made.

### Write what you had to dig for

Every trigger above is something the *user* did. This one is about you.

If you established something by reading code, running an experiment, or ruling
out a wrong answer — how a mechanism actually works, why the obvious fix does
not work, what a confusing result really meant — **write it down before you move
on.**

That research is the most expensive thing in the session and the easiest to
lose. The next agent starts with none of it and pays the same cost again: the
same files read, the same false leads followed, the same tokens spent reaching
the same conclusion. Half an hour of digging is worth one `remember` call.

Save the conclusion and what makes it true — the mechanism, the file that
decides it, the measurement — not the transcript of getting there. A finding
that reversed something you believed earlier is worth *more* than a
confirmation, not less: record what was wrong and what actually holds.

### Especially around subagents and workflows

**A subagent cannot see any of this.** Not this skill, not the block in
`CLAUDE.md`, not the vault. Its entire world is the prompt you write it. So the
instruction does not travel down that edge unless you carry it:

- put **"search Kaleidoscope before you start"** and **"record what you
  establish before you return"** into the prompt itself, next to whatever else
  that agent needs to know
- if you forgot, write the findings yourself the moment the agent returns —
  while you still have its report in front of you

A workflow is the worst place to skip this and the easiest place to skip it. It
is where the most research per token in a whole session happens: you fan out to
gather what you do not know, derive something from it, and decide what to do
next. By default none of that is kept. The parent receives a summary, the
reasoning is discarded with the transcript, and the next session starts from
nothing and pays to derive it again.

The asymmetry is what makes it worth a rule: **carrying the instruction costs
two lines in a prompt you were already writing. Not carrying it costs the whole
investigation.**

A write looks like this, and this exact payload works:

```json
{
  "mode": "create",
  "content_md": "# We chose Postgres over DynamoDB\n\nRelational queries across orders and users were the deciding factor; the team already runs Postgres in two other services.",
  "semantic_delta": {
    "memory_type": "decision",
    "title": "We chose Postgres over DynamoDB",
    "facts": [
      {"subject": "the orders service", "predicate": "stores_data_in", "object": "postgres"},
      {"subject": "the team", "predicate": "rejected", "object": "dynamodb"}
    ],
    "entities": [
      {"n": "the orders service", "kind": "artifact", "is": "the service that owns order records in this repository"},
      {"n": "postgres", "kind": "tool", "is": "the relational database chosen for primary storage"},
      {"n": "dynamodb", "kind": "tool", "is": "the key-value store considered and rejected"},
      {"n": "the team", "kind": "org", "is": "the engineers working on this repository"}
    ]
  }
}
```

Four things are worth knowing, because they are easy to get wrong:

- **Write the `title` yourself.** It is not taken from your markdown.
- **Every entity needs an `is`.** It is not a comment — it is how Kaleidoscope
  works out whether your "postgres" is the same thing as one written last month.
  A vague gloss makes a worse match.
- **Dates are not entities.** Put them in `occurred_at`, or a fact's
  `from`/`until`. Work out the actual date yourself; the store does not read
  "last Tuesday".
- **To change your mind, revise the memory** rather than writing a second one
  that contradicts the first. Use `mode: "update"`, or `corrections` and
  `contradicts`.

Got several things to record from one piece of work? Send them as separate
items in one call — one memory per idea, so each can be corrected later on its
own. Do not mash unrelated findings together to save a call.

`kscope schema remember` prints the full contract with every accepted value. It
is the authority; prefer it to any document, including this one.

## What not to save

- secrets, credentials, API keys, tokens
- transcripts of the conversation
- ordinary file contents, logs, command output
- anything the code or git history already records
- ideas you are still turning over — wait until they settle

If you would not want to read it back in three months, do not write it.

## When something goes wrong

**A refused call tells you what to fix.** It names the field and usually the
corrected value. Fix it and send it again.

One refusal is never a reason to stop using memory for the rest of the session.
That is the single most expensive mistake you can make here: the user loses
everything the rest of the session would have remembered, and they will not know
it happened.

If the tools genuinely are not there, carry on with the task, tell the user that
memory was unreachable so they can fix it, and do not invent memory operations.

## Before you finish

Take one look back: did this task settle anything a future session would
otherwise have to work out again? If so, write it now.

If nothing durable happened, write nothing. A memory that says "I did some work"
helps no one.

---

# Full CLI help text

URL: https://memory.kleosresearch.xyz/reference/kaleidoscope-cli.txt

Kaleidoscope local memory runtime

Usage:

AGENT -- the whole surface an agent needs. Two verbs, one door.

  kscope call search                         read;  one JSON request on stdin
  kscope call remember                       write; one JSON request on stdin
  kscope schema remember                     the write contract, before writing
  kscope schema [OPERATION]                  every operation this build has

  Those two resolve the vault from this directory. Name another one with
  `--profile`, which is what an editor or harness is started with:

  kscope call --profile <NAME> search
  kscope call --profile <NAME> remember

Everything below is an OPERATOR command: setup, inspection, and vault
lifecycle, run by a person or an installer and not by the agent using the
vault. `search` and `remember` are the only two published as MCP tools, and
the only two an agent is ever expected to choose between.

OPERATOR -- what this build is

  kscope --help
  kscope --version
  kscope model
  kscope gate
  kscope activate
  kscope licences
  kscope public-contract

OPERATOR -- bring a vault into existence

  kscope init [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope init <ROOT> <RFC3339_CREATED_AT> [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope init-profile <NAME> <ROOT> <RFC3339_CREATED_AT> [process-local|durable-local]

OPERATOR -- profiles, a named non-secret pointer to one vault

  kscope profile create <NAME> <ROOT> <WORKSPACE_ID> <PRINCIPAL_ID> <JOURNAL> [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope profile import <NAME> <ROOT> [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope profile list
  kscope profile show <NAME>
  kscope profile remove <NAME>
  kscope profile launch <NAME>

OPERATOR -- which vault a command that names none resolves to

  kscope where
  kscope where --root-only

OPERATOR -- maintain a local vault

  kscope vault-migrate <ROOT>
  kscope vault-verify <ROOT> [--cross-backend]
  kscope vault-preview <ROOT>
  kscope vault-delete <ROOT>

OPERATOR -- encrypted repository vaults, a frozen macOS preview

  kscope vault-create <REPOSITORY> <RFC3339_CREATED_AT>
  kscope vault-open <REPOSITORY>
  kscope vault-close <REPOSITORY>
  kscope vault-recover <REPOSITORY>
  kscope vault-export-device <REPOSITORY> <NEW_PACKAGE_DIRECTORY>
  kscope vault-import-device <PACKAGE_DIRECTORY> <REPOSITORY>
  kscope vault-encrypted-preview <REPOSITORY>
  kscope vault-encrypted-delete <REPOSITORY>

OPERATOR -- run an engine for an agent, addressed three ways

  kscope mcp --profile <NAME>
  kscope serve --profile <NAME>
  kscope context --profile <NAME>
  kscope call --profile <NAME> <OPERATION>

  kscope mcp [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope serve [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope context [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope call <OPERATION> [process-local|durable-local]

  kscope mcp <ROOT> <WORKSPACE_ID> <PRINCIPAL_ID> <JOURNAL> [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope serve <ROOT> <WORKSPACE_ID> <PRINCIPAL_ID> <JOURNAL> [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope context <ROOT> <WORKSPACE_ID> <PRINCIPAL_ID> <JOURNAL> [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope call <ROOT> <WORKSPACE_ID> <PRINCIPAL_ID> <JOURNAL> <OPERATION> [process-local|durable-local]

The four commands that address a vault accept the four ids or none of them.
Naming none resolves them: KSCOPE_ROOT, else `.kaleidoscope/` under the
repository's main checkout, else `.kaleidoscope/` under the working directory --
and then the vault's own workspace record for the workspace, principal and
journal, so naming the root names all four. KSCOPE_WORKSPACE,
KSCOPE_PRINCIPAL and KSCOPE_JOURNAL override that record field by field, and
are how a vault holding more than one workspace is disambiguated.

Arguments always win, and win completely: an invocation naming the four ids
never reads the environment at all. That is what keeps every existing caller
byte-identical.

A resolved root that is not a vault is REFUSED by those four commands, naming
the path and where the path came from. They never create one: `kscope init` is
the only way a vault comes into existence, because a wrong root is not an
error, it is a different vault.

Init itself accepts the same two shapes. Naming ROOT and RFC3339_CREATED_AT is
unchanged in every respect, and is what a harness uses when a vault's created_at
has to be controlled. Naming neither resolves the root by the rules above, uses
the current time, and defaults to process-local -- durable-local fresh-root
initialization is refused before any effect, so it is asked for rather than
defaulted to. The resolved root and its provenance are printed on stderr,
unprompted.

A resolved root that is ALREADY a vault is refused too, and nothing there is
touched: a second init on an existing root mints a fresh workspace inside it,
and a vault holding two workspaces can no longer be addressed without naming
one. The refusal reports the ids it already has.

The resolved form also ensures the repository ignores the vault. `git
check-ignore` decides whether an existing rule already covers it, in which case
nothing is written; otherwise one commented rule is APPENDED, never reordering
or rewriting the file, and never adding a trailing newline the file did not
have. Outside a git repository nothing is written and no repository is created;
the vault is simply reported as not ignored. What was done is named on stderr
and in the gitignore field on stdout.

A version-1 profile is a non-secret pointer to one existing vault identity. It
stores an absolute root, workspace, principal, journal and durability under the
platform configuration directory's `kaleidoscope/profiles`, or exactly under
KSCOPE_PROFILE_HOME when that override is set. Profile names are portable and
path-safe; profile files are atomic, owner-only on Unix and validated against
the vault each time they are loaded. `profile import` derives the identity from
the selected vault; `profile create` verifies the explicit tuple. Neither one
creates or relocates canonical vault data.

`init-profile` is the native fresh-bootstrap primitive. It initializes the
explicit root, then writes the named profile. If the second step fails, it does
not delete the committed vault; the refusal reports the exact root and a
machine-readable recovery argv for `kscope profile import`. Durable-local is
never silently downgraded and remains refused before initialization effects.

`profile launch` prints a versioned stdio launch descriptor pointing directly
at this absolute engine executable with `mcp --profile NAME`. The descriptor
names only `search` and `remember` and contains no vault coordinates or secret.
Explicit four-coordinate invocations remain the compatibility authority and do
not read KSCOPE_PROFILE_HOME.

The where command prints the address these rules resolve to, as JSON, and
resolves nothing else. Every command that resolved rather than was told also
prints the same on stderr, unprompted, because a caller relying on a default
cannot check a root it did not type. stdout stays exactly what it was.

The licences command prints the attribution for third-party material this
executable redistributes inside itself. The embedded embedding table is
MinishLab's, under MIT, and MIT requires its notice to accompany every copy --
which a one-file release cannot do with a NOTICE beside the binary. `licenses`
is accepted as a spelling. The output states what it does not yet cover.

The model command prints one JSON object naming the semantic embedding model
this executable carries, its table dtype, and the SHA-256 of its two files, or
reports that this build has none. A release must report one: the release
installer refuses a package whose executable does not.

The gate command prints one JSON object naming what this build carries of the
alpha entitlement gate: enforcing or absent, the commands the gate refuses,
and where a key file would be read from. It reads no key, opens no vault and
reports no authorization decision. The gate never refuses this command, so an
operator holding a refused binary can still find out why it was refused.

The activate command is how a machine becomes entitled. It takes the key from
KALEIDOSCOPE_API_KEY, from the key file, or from standard input; stores it at
the path the gate command reports, so an engine a host starts with an empty
environment finds it; and waits for the verdict rather than leaving the next
command to discover an empty cache. It is never gated, because a gate across
the only route to becoming entitled is closed to everyone not already through
it. It exits 0 only when the key reached the disk: a key that could not be
stored is a refusal naming the path, and a build carrying no gate refuses as
well rather than reporting an activation it did not perform.

`-h` and `-V` are accepted as short forms of `--help` and `--version`.

The public-contract command prints a small source-free JSON seed for release
contract generation. It opens no vault and loads no model.

The vault-recover command reads a JSON object containing recovery_key from
stdin. The two delete commands require their preview command's
confirmation_token in a JSON object on stdin. Encrypted repository vaults are
a frozen macOS-preview feature.

The optional serve command uses a Unix-domain socket and is unavailable on
non-Unix platforms. The stdio mcp command and process-scoped call command do
not depend on it.

The vault-migrate command builds the storage engine's index over a vault
written by the older fs-v0 engine. It creates, moves, copies and deletes no
content file, re-runs safely, works on a vault whose journal has rotated, and
is undone by deleting one file -- until the first write through the engine.
Run vault-verify after it and before writing. Neither command reads the
journal, so both work on a vault this executable cannot otherwise open.

The context command reads one search JSON request from stdin and prints only
the concise model-visible memory text. call search returns the bounded public
result, including final rank and fused score on selected hits; private
policy/ranker feature vectors, the signed decision payload and engine
diagnostics are omitted. The documented public workflow has no supported
outcome-attribution path until a future authenticated manager/controller
interface exchanges a keyed opaque handle. This is an API contract, not an
authentication claim about the local vault.

The call command reads one JSON request from stdin. OPERATION is one of:

  AGENT     search | remember
  OPERATOR  feedback | memory_lifecycle | memory_import | address_maintenance
            maintenance | ontology | doctor

Only the two agent verbs are published as MCP tools. search merges what were
recall, compile and read_memory: a query ranks and a memory_id addresses. A
ranked search always writes the exposure row and bounds the served set --
ledger: false was a second door and is refused, so a measurement that must not
write to a vault has to clone it first. Its four knobs are top_k,
candidate_pool, bfs_depth and max_facts, each with a published default and
ceiling.

The schema command prints one OPERATION's full descriptive parameters and
closed values. MCP derives a versioned compact, omission-first inputSchema from
the same operation semantics. The two preserve the same non-null machine
constraints but are intentionally not byte-identical: the native decoder
accepts legacy explicit null while MCP omits absent optionals. Pass no OPERATION
to list them.

Exit codes. 0 means applied: everything asked for happened, and for a remember
carrying items every submitted item was written. 2 means refused: nothing was
applied, stdout carries a refusal envelope rather than a per-item report, and
the repair is to fix the request and re-send it whole. 3 means applied in part:
the response says status partial, some items were written and at least one was
not, and stdout carries results -- one entry per submitted item, in submission
order, each with its own status and reason. Re-send only the items whose status
is not a write; re-sending the batch re-submits memories the vault already
holds. 3 exists so that a caller reading $? can tell those two repairs apart
without parsing the body, which is the parse an exit code exists to avoid.

---

{
  "checked against": "kscope 0.0.5, on 2026-08-31. The two field lists below are the `inputSchema` of each tool in the `tools/list` result of `kscope mcp`. That command needs a key, so every statement here was also checked against three that do not: `kscope schema search` and `kscope schema remember` print the same two field sets, and `kscope public-contract` prints the batch bound, the stdio transport, and `operator_commands_in_mcp: false`.   "what this is not": "The schema itself. This file is written here and checked against the engine; the engine's tools/list is the authority, and a build may accept less than this file lists. Read the schema your own host discovered before you rely on a field. Two fields that `kscope --help` names as knobs of the command-line `call search` -- bfs_depth and max_facts -- are refused by the MCP inputSchema and are therefore absent above. Whether Kaleidoscope is released, and to whom, is not stated here: that is one fact and it lives in the release metadata this site is built from."
